Porsche Mission S Hits the Streets of New York for the First Time
18 photos
Photo: Porsche | Instagram
The all-new Porsche Mission S has just hit the streets of New York. The concept car moved from its world premiere stage onto the public roads of Manhattan and Brooklyn. Official photos show it navigating real NYC traffic near the High Line and across the DUMBO trendy neighborhood.
Porsche's new supercar concept rides low, wide, and aggressively aerodynamic, seemingly trying but failing to fly under the radar. With that striking silhouette finished in silver, it is next to impossible for the Mission S to keep a low profile.
Porsche chose New York for the premiere of its Mission S on October 15. The official unveiling of the concept car took place at the Sound River Studios, a waterfront venue located on a historic pier in Long Island City in Queens.
Porsche deliberately chose this exact location for the event for its historical significance: it is the exact same Queens pier where the first global press photos of the iconic mid-engined Porsche 550 Spyder were taken back in 1953.
The Mission S shares a direct spiritual and engineering connection with the 550 Spyder. While their tech is decades apart, Porsche designed the Mission S as a nod to its 1950s ancestor in terms of engineering, design cues, and cockpit layout.
Just like the 1953 Porsche 550 Spyder, the Mission S comes with a mid-engine architecture. By putting the engine in the middle, the automaker altered the typical supercar proportions in favor of a balanced stance, designed entirely for performance.
Furthermore, the all-new supercar features prominent “torpedo” fenders that rise higher than the front hood. It is a classic Porsche design cue that started with the brand’s earliest race cars, including the 550 Spyder and the 356, allowing the driver to see the edges of the front wheels from the cockpit.
In the meantime, the top-mounted cooling fan echoes the iconic design of the 917 , which gave Porsche its first overall win at the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1970 and 1971. Meanwhile, the "telephone dial" wheels are a throwback to the 928 luxury grand tourer, which debuted in 1977 as a 1978 model year.
Porsche hasn’t disclosed any details about the engine that powers the Mission S , but the automaker is reportedly secretly developing an all-new flat-eight engine specifically for the production version of this concept car.
The photos taken in New York show the concept car in motion, so it has to have something behind the seats, unless Porsche is trying to trick us by showing us an empty shell photoshopped with the motion effect to make us believe that it really is moving on its own power. One thing is for sure: it will not be an EV.
When will the production version arrive? Porsche is keeping that information under wraps as well. The only thing leaked about this car was the footage that showed up online just hours before the global premiere last week, and that was it.
